newsitem.title: USA: Judge denies request for delay in Okla. bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Judge denies request for delay in Okla. bombing case.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing case on Tuesday denied a request by attorneys for defendant Timothy McVeigh to delay the trial because of heavy publicity on the second anniversary of the tragedy.

U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch also denied several other legal motions made by defence attorneys, including one seeking to increase to 40 from 23 the number of so-called peremptory challenges the defence has in selecting the jury of 12 panellists and six alternates. Such challenges allow each side to dismiss potential jurors without naming a specific reason.
Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said a delay was necessary due to "a series of what can only be called massive media portrayals of the second anniversay of the Oklahoma City bombing."

Jones said while observances of the anniversary last Saturday in Denver and around the nation were appropriate, they took place during "a sensitive period" when potenial jurors were being interviewed. The observance in Denver included the ringing of church bells 168 times, one for each of the bombing victims.
The defence attorney did not specify how long he wanted the trial delayed.
Denying the request during the brief, 10-minute hearing, the judge replied: "I don't think any time is necessary."
Later in the morning, prosecutors and attorneys were slated to begin making the peremptory challenges.

Those chosen for the jury will hear the highly emotional case against McVeigh, who is charged with bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995. The worst-ever attack on civilians on U.S. soil killed 168 people, including 19 children.
McVeigh, a Gulf War veteran, has pleaded not guilty. He faces the death penalty if convicted.

Ninety-nine potential jurors have been questioned since the proceedings began on March 31. The judge has kept their identities secret, assigning them numbers, seating them behind a panel in the courtroom and omitting identifying details in his conversations with them.
Opening arguments are expected to begin on Thursday, leaving Wednesday as a day off for jurors to set their personal affairs in order.
Lead prosecutor Joseph Hartzler is expected to make the opening statement for the prosecution, laying out the government's case.
